paper_title: Structured Confidence Perturbation via Fisher Geometry for Adversarial Training

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Adversarial training is often plagued by "pseudo-attacks", perturbations that significantly increase the loss value but fail to truly alter the model's confidence structure. To address this, we propose two complementary approaches to directly attack and defend against confidence structure deformation. First, building upon the traditional loss maximization perspective, we introduce a hybrid objective that integrates cross-entropy and KL divergence, encouraging adversarial examples to simultaneously disrupt prediction accuracy and distribution consistency. Second, we geometrically reconstruct adversarial training by generating perturbations that maximize the distribution distance on the confidence manifold. Theoretical analysis shows that the optimal perturbation direction aligns with the principal eigenvectors of the Fisher information matrix. We also propose an efficient algorithm to avoid high-dimensional matrix computations. Experiments on multiple datasets and model architectures demonstrate that our method outperforms existing methods in adversarial robustness and robust transferability, particularly excelling in structural perturbations within high-confidence regions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable progress across numerous applications; however, despite their impressive performance, they remain highly susceptible to adversarial perturbations which conduct imperceptible modifications to inputs that cause incorrect predictions [1]. This vulnerability has raised significant concerns in safetycritical domains such as image recognition [2], autonomous driving [3], and anomaly detection [4]. Among various defense strategies, adversarial training has emerged as one of the most effective methods for improving model robustness [5, 6]. By jointly optimizing over clean and adversarial samples, it encourages models to learn stable decision boundaries under input perturbations. Corresponding author. Preprint. Existing adversarial training methods are commonly grouped into gradient-based approaches, optimization-based formulations, and attack-driven adversarial sample generation. Gradient-based methods such as FGSM and PGD [7, 8] construct perturbations by following the loss gradient, offering high computational efficiency but ensuring robustness only in local linear neighborhood. Optimization-based defenses treat adversarial training as minmax problem and explicitly minimize the worst-case loss under bounded perturbations, often using solvers like L-BFGS [9] or zero-order optimization [10]; however, their computational overhead is typically prohibitive for large-scale models. Meanwhile, adversarial attackbased methods [11] generate perturbed samples directly by designing black-box or white-box attacks: black-box methods rely solely on model outputs, whereas white-box attacks exploit full model gradients and internal structures. Prevailing adversarial training methods largely share common heuristic: they craft perturbations by maximizing the classification loss with respect to the true label. While effective in reducing the predicted probability of the true class, this loss-centric paradigm often fails to induce meaningful, global changes in the models output distribution. As illustrated in Fig. 1, even when the loss is increased, the relative ordering of confidence across classes may remain intacta phenomenon we term pseudo-attacks. We define "pseudo-attack" as perturbation δ satisfying L(x + δ, y) > L(x, y) but arg maxk p(y = kx + δ) = arg maxk p(y = kx). Even if the top-1 remains unchanged, the relative confidence ranking and distribution shape can still maintain local stability, meaning that the geometric vulnerability of the model near the decision boundary is not truly challenged. Such perturbations do not genuinely challenge the structural geometry of the models confidence manifold, leaving underlying vulnerabilities exposed. Figure 1: Most previous methods add perturbation noise to single discriminant value (x) for adversarial training (top), while our SCP adds structured perturbations to the statistical manifold {p(yx; θ)x X} for adversarial training (bottom). To move beyond local loss maximization, we argue that adversarial robustness should be grounded in the geometric stability of the models confidence distribution. In this paper, we introduce unified adversarial training framework that operates directly on the statistical manifold of output probabilities. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We propose an enhanced Single Point Perturbation (SPP) strategy that combines crossentropy (CE) and KullbackLeibler (KL) divergence into hybrid objective. Unlike prior uses of KL as regularizer [12], we deploy it actively during attack generation to disrupt both the top-1 prediction and the overall confidence structure. We develop SCP framework that reformulates adversarial search as maximizing the distance between probability distributions on the confidence manifold. We show theoretically that the optimal perturbation aligns with the principal eigenvector of the Fisher Information 2 Matrix (FIM), which captures the local curvature of the manifold. To enable scalable computation, we derive an efficient eigen-decomposition that avoids explicit manipulation of high-dimensional FIM. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet demonstrate that our methods consistently improve adversarial robustness and enhance attack transferability across architectures. By directly targeting the geometric roots of model vulnerability, SCP and SPP advance the state of the art in adversarial training, offering principled and computationally feasible path toward truly robust deep learning systems.

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Adversarial Training and Geometry. Adversarial training (AT) has evolved from local noise defense strategy into holistic paradigm that reshapes the decision manifold of deep neural networks. Early mainstream gradient-based methods, such as FGSM [7] and PGD [8], primarily constructed adversarial perturbations within local ϵ-sphere along the direction of steepest loss increase. While effective, their robustness was often limited to these direct input neighborhoods. To seek more globally stable solutions, optimization-based frameworks [8, 12] modeled adversarial training as minimax game. Although subsequent acceleration strategies, such as FreeAT [13], YOPO [14], improved training efficiency, they essentially still followed the same loss-centric heuristic. In recent years, some methods, including feature scattering [15] and MART [16], have attempted to learn more transferable features through feature space alignment or hard example reweighting, but they often neglect the underlying geometry of the data manifold. Many existing approaches rely on maximizing the cross-entropy (CE) loss to measure adversarial vulnerability, while methods such as TRADES maximize distributional discrepancy during attack generation. This approach is essentially pointwise suppression of the true logit, which typically fails to induce global distortion of the models confidence structure. While TRADES [12] and ensemble-based approaches [17] introduce KL divergence or diversity constraints, they generally treat distributional disparity as scalar penalty rather than structural measure. Our work breaks with this convention by redefining adversarial perturbations as geometric transformations on the confidence manifold and asserting that true robustness stems from the manifolds geometric stability under structural stress. Information-Theoretic Perspectives. The application of KL divergence in adversarial training has traditionally been limited to its use as scalar measure of distributional disparity. common practice is to use it as consistency regularization term to balance the tradeoff between natural accuracy and adversarial robustness (e.g., TRADES [12] or gradient-smoothing approaches [18]). Another perspective stems from knowledge distillation, where KL divergence guides distribution alignment [19], thereby facilitating the learning of robust representations. However, most of these paradigms overlook the profound informational geometric meaning of KL divergence. Within the informational geometry framework, the KL divergence between two neighboring probability distributions is equivalent to second-order approximation of the Mahalanobis distance defined by the Fisher information matrix (FIM). Existing defense methods utilize its size for constraint but fail to fully leverage its potential as tool for discovering structured vulnerabilities. Our research bridges this gap by transforming KL divergence from passive regularization term into an active target for attack generation. By maximizing the manifold distance along the Fisher principal eigenvectors, we can systematically disrupt the global structure of the confidence distribution, rather than merely suppressing local outputs, forcing the model to learn more resilient geometric representation and effectively overcoming the evaluation blind spots inherent in traditional paradigms.

sections.title: 3 Methodology
sections.content: Traditional adversarial training generates perturbations by maximizing the loss function (e.g., crossentropy CE), but such methods only locally suppress the logit of the true class, ignoring the global geometry of the confidence distribution  (Fig. 1)  . We propose that true robustness should stem from the models stability on the confidence manifold, i.e., the input perturbation should maximize the struc3 tural deformation of the output probability distribution. To this end, we design two complementary strategies: Local Single-Point Perturbation (SPP): Jointly optimizes CE and KL divergence, simultaneously disrupting prediction accuracy and distribution consistency; Global Structured Confidence Perturbation (SCP): From an information geometry perspective, it generates perturbations using the principal eigendirections of the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM), directly manipulating the curvature of the confidence manifold. 3.1 Geometric motivation: from single points to manifold deformation Let the model be fθ : RK, where θ denotes the parameters and is the number of classes. sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: 4.1 Datasets and settings We used three common and popular datasets for image classification: CIFAR-10 [20], CIFAR-100 [20], and Tiny-ImageNet [21]. CIFAR-10 contains 60,000 color images of size 32 32 in 10 categories. CIFAR-100 contains 60,000 color images of size 32 32 in 100 categories. TinyImageNet is subset of ImageNet [22] with 200 categories, similar to the ImageNet dataset, where each category contains 500 color images of size 64 64. To comprehensively evaluate the relationship between model geometry and attack resistance, we conduct experiments on representative architectures with distinct structural characteristics: ResNet[23]: It introduces residual connections, allowing gradients to bypass nonlinear layers directly. Skip connections stabilize the gradient flow, reduce gradient vanishing/explosion, and reduce variance, so its maximum eigenvalue is relatively low. DenseNet[24]: Each layer of DenseNet receives the output of all previous layers as input. With more gradient paths and gradients dispersed to each layer, its variance is potentially the smallest among the considered models. ViT[25]: Vision Transformer (ViT) is based on the self-attention mechanism, which causes the gradient to involve global interactions, potentially introducing large variance; however, LayerNorm and residual connections help stabilize the gradient. The batch size on each dataset is 32, the learning rate η is 3 104 , and the maximum perturbation range coefficient ϵ is 8/255 in training section. The adversarial training contains 100 epochs. All experiments were conducted on server equipped with six NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPUs. At the same time, we introduce CW[26] and AutoAttack[27] as our counter-test methods. We test our SCP method on multiple datasets and baseline models. The specific parameters of AutoAttack are ϵ = 0.5, the type of norm is L2; the parameter settings of the CW-10 method are as follows: the learning rate is 0.01, the confidence threshold is 0, and the number of iterations is 10. 4.2 Evaluation metrics Assume that the test set is D, the set of all instances predicted correctly by the model is , and a(x) represents the perturbed sample generated by the clean input x. We can define the following three main metrics: STD, ADV, and ASR: Standard Accuracy (STD) [28] represents the standard test accuracy of in-distribution generalization, which is the accuracy obtained by testing the model using the original test sample, i.e, STD = D . Adversarial Robust Accuracy (ADV) Adversarial robust accuracy is method used to evaluate the performance of model when facing adversarial samples. When we use dataset consisting of perturbed samples generated by test samples to test the model obtained through adversarial training, the classification accuracy obtained is called ADV accuracy. In our (x,y)T (a(x))=y experiments with attack methods AutoAttack, it is defined as ADV = (cid:80) . Attack Success Rate (ASR) ASR measures the proportion of samples that an attacker can cause the model to make incorrect predictions and is used to measure the robustness of the model. It is worth noting that for the above three measurements, using the ADV under AutoAttack, we have the following relationship ASR = 1 ADV STD . 4.3 Comparison on attack metrics We compare our SCP algorithm with state-of-the-art (SOTA) adversarial training methods on three widely used image classification datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet) using ResNet18, ResNet34, and ResNet50 [23] as baseline models. These architectures were chosen as the common intersection of models used in recent adversarial training literature, balancing computational efficiency and representativeness. Driven by its geometric approach to perturbing the belief manifold rather than traditional scalar loss optimization, SCP demonstrates competitive performance, particularly on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets. As shown in Table 1, SCP frequently achieves the highest robust accuracy under AutoAttack (AA). For instance, on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-50, SCP achieves an AA of 72.50%, surpassing SPP (70.99%) and significantly outperforming baseline methods. Conversely, SPP exhibits superior performance on the Tiny-ImageNet dataset. Across all three ResNet architectures on TinyImageNet, SPP yields higher Standard Accuracy (STD) than SCP. Its Attack Success Rate (ASR) is lower on ResNet-18 and ResNet-50; on ResNet-34, SPP has an ASR of 30.69%, compared with SCPs 28.89%. From dataset perspective, SCP consistently minimizes the Attack Success Rate (ASR) compared to traditional methods like PGD and TRADES, validating its focus on structured belief perturbations over heuristic input space attacks. This advantage is most performed on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. For example, using the ResNet-50 architecture on CIFAR-10, SCP achieves remarkable ASR of 12.90%, which is substantial improvement over TRADES (19.34%) and PGD (17.10%). Even on the more challenging CIFAR-100 dataset, SCP maintains this robust superiority; with ResNet-50, it suppresses the ASR to 24.59%, whereas competitive baselines like MIFGSM and PIFGSM struggle with ASRs of 29.65% and 30.32%, respectively. The proposed methods, SPP and SCP, perform exceptionally well across varying model depths: ResNet-18, ResNet-34, and ResNet-50, demonstrating that the geometric disruption of the belief manifold scales effectively with network complexity. On Tiny-ImageNet, SCP has lower STD than SPP at all three depths and higher ASR at two of the three depths. We attribute this behavior to three factors. First, the large number of classes (200) inflates the estimation variance of the Fisher Information Matrix, degrading the accuracy of its principal eigenvector. Second, the underfitting on this dataset may violate SCPs assumption of well-converged confidence manifold, making its single-step perturbation unreliable. Third, SPPs multi-step signed gradient updates are inherently more robust to gradient noise and do not rely on explicit geometric estimation, offering greater stability under challenging training conditions. 4.4 Comparison with recent baselines We further compare our methods with recent adversarial training baselines under the CIFAR-10 setting. As shown in Table 2, the proposed methods remain highly competitive against recent adversarial training baselines under the AutoAttack evaluation. SCP achieves the best robust accuracy of 70.47%, while SPP obtains the second-best result of 70.15%, both surpassing the strongest non-ours baseline GAWP (68.89%). SPP and SCP also reduce ASR to 14.35% and 14.78%, respectively, compared with RAMPs 18.88%. These results indicate that our confidence-geometry-based training improves robustness rather than merely increasing clean accuracy. 4.5 Cross-architecture evaluation To comprehensively evaluate the relationship between model geometry and attack resistance, we conduct experiments on representative architectures with distinct structural characteristics, as shown in Table 3: For DenseNet121, both SPP and SCP maintain their superiority, with SCP achieving an outstanding STD of 82.49% and robust AA of 69.79%. This aligns with our expectations: DenseNets dense skip connections disperse gradient flow across layers, effectively minimizing gradient variance and 9 providing stable, smooth geometric manifold that perfectly suits our covariance-based perturbation estimation. Conversely, on the ViT-B/16 architecture, we observe systemic performance degradation across all evaluated adversarial training methods, including our SPP/SCP and established baselines like TRADES and PIFGSM. The standard accuracy (STD) and robust accuracy (AA) for all methods drop significantly compared to their CNN counterparts. We attribute this phenomenon to two fundamental conflicts between the ViT architecture and current gradient-based adversarial training paradigms: Lack of Local Inductive Bias and Severe Underfitting: Unlike CNNs, ViTs lack translational invariance and local inductive biases. They are notoriously data-hungry and prone to severe underfitting when trained from scratch on small-scale datasets like CIFAR-10. Introducing strong adversarial constraints (whether through TRADES KL-divergence or our geometric manifold perturbations) acts as an excessive regularization that further chokes the models representation capacity, leading to the observed collapse in STD. High Gradient Variance and Manifold Instability: ViTs rely heavily on global self-attention mechanisms, meaning that spatial perturbations interact globally across the entire image patch sequence. This global interaction induces highly non-local and high-variance gradients. Since almost all current adversarial training methods (especially our SCP, which relies on the Fisher Information Matrix for local geometric approximation) depend on stable local gradient information, the noisy gradient landscape of ViT causes the estimated worst-case perturbation directions to become highly inaccurate. This instability explains why neither traditional PGD-based methods nor our covariance-guided framework can achieve optimal robustness on Vision Transformers without specialized architectural adaptations. 4.6 Diagnostic analysis on ViT-B/ To provide direct evidence for the above explanation, we further measure gradient variation on CIFAR10. For each mini-batch b, we compute the mean input-gradient norm g(b) i=1 xiLb2. Their relative variation is computed as = 1 (cid:80)m RV(g) = stdb(g(b)) meanb(g(b)) , (14) where larger value indicates noisier gradient landscape across batches. As shown in Fig. 2, ViT-B/16 exhibits the largest input-gradient variation (0.345), compared with ResNet-18 (0.247) and DenseNet-121 (0.268). It also shows more dispersed FIM directionstability distribution than the CNN architectures. These observations support our claim that ViT-B/16 produces noisier local gradients and less reliable local geometric estimates, which weakens SCP on this architecture. 4.7 Cross-model transferability We next evaluate whether adversarial examples generated on one architecture can transfer to different target architectures. We use three ResNet-18 source models trained with PGD, TRADES, and PIFGSM, generate AutoAttack-L2 adversarial examples on CIFAR-10, and directly evaluate the same adversarial examples on DenseNet-121 and ViT-B/16 target models without re-optimizing them on the target models. This follows the standard black-box transfer setting [41]. Let be the test set, be target model, and xs,A adv be the adversarial example generated by attack on source model s. The Z-axis represents the models prediction confidence, defined as the maximum softmax probability of the predicted class. Figure 3 illustrates the distribution shift between clean samples and adversarial examples generated by CW[26] and our SCP method on the CIFAR-10 dataset. As shown in Figure 3, benign samples (represented by blue points) cluster into distinct regions and reside on high-confidence plateau, with Z-axis values consistently near 1.0. CW attack lead to many adversarial points remaining in high-confidence zones (represented by orange points). This phenomenon confirms the existence of pseudo-attacks, where the perturbation fails to disrupt the models belief structure fundamentally. In contrast, our SCP method induces much more radical deformation of the confidence landscape (represented by red points). The confidence scores for SCPgenerated samples drop sharply, indicating that our method effectively explores the most vulnerable regions of the statistical manifold. Figure 3: 3D visualization comparison of confidence shift on CIFAR-10 (left: CW, right: SCP). The X-Y plane represents t-SNE projected features, and the Z-axis represents the prediction confidence. 4.10 Time and space complexity We analyze the computational efficiency of SPP and SCP to demonstrate their practical feasibility. While SPP follows standard linear complexity, the primary bottleneck for SCP has been solved by using the decomposition technique; see Eq. (13). This approach ensures that our geometric paradigm remains scalable and feasible for large-scale deep learning systems. 4.11 Ablation study Effectiveness of Hybrid loss: To verify the effectiveness of the proposed hybrid loss function, we present comparison in Table 7 among the PGD (CE only), the TRADES (KL only), and our proposed hybrid loss SPP (CE+KL) on the CIFAR10 dataset using ResNet-18. As shown in Table 1, the proposed hybrid loss strategy achieves superior performance across all metrics compared with using either loss component individually. The SPP (CE+KL) method achieves the highest Clean Accuracy of 81.90% and the highest AutoAttack accuracy of 70.15%. This represents significant improvement over the CE-only baseline and also outperforms the KL-only approach. In terms of ASR, the hybrid loss achieves the strongest defense, reducing ASR to 14.35%. This is notably lower than both the CE-only (20.92%) and KL-only (19.56%) configurations. These results confirm that combining CE and KL losses allows the model to learn more robust features without compromising standard accuracy, demonstrating the effectiveness of the SPP hybrid loss design. Loss Type Clean Acc AA ASR CE only KL only CE + KL (SPP) 78.87% 80.72% 81.90% 62.37% 20.92% 64.93% 19.56% 70.15% 14.35% We further analyze the sensitivity of SPP to the KL-loss weight. In this experiment, the SPP training objective is LSPP = LCE + λLKL, (17) where λ controls the contribution of the distribution-consistency term. We train ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 with λ {0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0} and evaluate the trained models under clean, PGD, CW-10, and AutoAttack-L2 settings. As shown in Fig. 4, the SPP performance is stable across broad range of λ. The clean and attack accuracies fluctuate only mildly, indicating that the CE and KL terms are complementary rather than requiring fragile tuning. In particular, λ = 1.0 gives the best clean and CW-10 performance, while λ = 2.0 achieves the best accuracy. 13 Figure 4: SPP lambda ablation on CIFAR-10 using ResNet-18.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We address the pseudo-attack problem using two complementary approachesSingle Point Perturbation (SPP) and Structured Confidence Perturbation (SCP)systematically attacking and strengthening the models confidence structure stability from two levels: local sample-level perturbation and global manifold-level deformation, respectively. SPP integrates hybrid loss function combining CE and KL, while SCP further models adversarial perturbation as distance maximization problem on the confidence manifold from an information geometry perspective. SCPs scalable computation makes it suitable for large-scale classification tasks. Experimental results show that the proposed method significantly improves adversarial robustness on multiple standard datasets and model architectures. Visualization analysis further confirms that SCP effectively induces global deformation of the confidence distribution, preventing adversarial examples from remaining in high-confidence regions. Future research directions include exploring its potential to improve robustness in generative models and self-supervised learning.
